---
title: "Quiz: geodesic active contours"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Edge-stopping function $g = 1/(1 + |\nabla I_\sigma|^2/k^2)$; speed $F = g(c - \varepsilon\kappa)$ plus advection along $-\nabla g$.

---

**Q1.** With $k = 10$, what is $g$ where $|\nabla I_\sigma| = 0$, $10$ and $30$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Plug in: $1/(1 + (m/k)^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
1, 0.5 and 0.1. Flat regions let the front move at full speed; an edge three times stronger than $k$ slows it to 10%.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why smooth the image (σ > 0) before computing $g$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the gradient of pure noise look like?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Differences of neighbouring noisy pixels are large, so without smoothing $g$ is small at many pixels inside flat regions: the front gets stuck on noise. Smoothing averages the noise away while keeping large-scale edges (at the cost of blurring nearby edges together).
:::

---

**Q3.** A balloon front ($F = g c$, no advection) reaches an edge where $g = 0.05$. Does it stop?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Is the speed zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: it slows to 5% of $c$ but keeps creeping, and after enough time it crosses the edge. Only $g = 0$ exactly would stop it. The advection term of geodesic active contours pulls it back into the edge.
:::

---

**Q4.** In which direction does $-\nabla g$ point on each side of an edge?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$g$ has a valley at the edge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Towards the edge from both sides: $g$ decreases towards the bottom of the valley, so $-\nabla g$ points downhill, into the edge. A front on either side is pushed onto it.
:::

---

**Q5.** What is the edge-weighted length $\oint g\,ds$ of a curve that runs exactly along an edge where $g = 0.05$, compared with a curve of the same length in a flat region?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each bit of curve costs $g$ times its length.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
5% of it. Along edges the curve is "short" in the image's metric, so the shortest closed curve (a geodesic) prefers to follow edges.
:::

---

**Q6.** A curve shrinks onto a C-shaped object from outside, with no balloon. Why does it not enter the slot of the C?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What drives the part of the curve that bridges the opening?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The bridging part is straight ($\kappa = 0$) and lies in a flat region ($g \approx 1$, $\nabla g \approx 0$): no curvature, no advection, no balloon: nothing moves it. A negative balloon $c$ pushes it into the slot.
:::

---

**Q7.** Starting from one curve around three separate objects, how many curves do you get, and who decides that?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall unit 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three (one per object, if the parameters are right). The zero level of $\phi$ splits by itself when it passes between the objects; neither the user nor the algorithm has to count the objects.
:::

---

**Q8.** Why does a large balloon leak through a weak part of an edge but not through a strong part?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $g c$ with the advection there.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a weak edge $g$ is not small (0.44 in the demo) and $\nabla g$ is shallow, so the balloon's push $g c$ beats the advection that pulls the front back; on a strong edge $g \approx 0$ and the valley is steep. Once the front passes the weak spot, it spreads into the region behind it.
:::
